sample_size.excerpt: We evaluated dietary beta-carotene and vitamin C in relation to subsequent risk of prostate cancer in a prospective study of 1,899 middle-aged men. We combined prostate cancer cases diagnosed in the first 24 years of follow-up with incident cases identified from the Health Care Financing Administration hospitalization and outpatient files during an additional 6-year follow-up period.

cases.excerpt: During the 30-year follow-up, prostate cancer developed in 132 men.

effect_size.excerpt: There was no indication that consumption of beta-carotene or vitamin C was related to increased or decreased risk of prostate cancer. headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 8 studies yielded an effect size of 0.96 (95% CI: 0.84–1.1), indicating no statistically significant association between Vitamin C and prostate cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by substantial heterogeneity (I² = 55.17%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
